subject: English Literature
source: AQA GCSE English Literature 8702 specification, Paper 1 Section A (Shakespeare: Macbeth) from own knowledge, continuing y10.json (A Christmas Carol, Section B). Drive reviewed: no Macbeth scheme of work found; the school reading policy places Macbeth in the Y10-11 pathway. Quotations are short fair-dealing extracts.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Macbeth - Context, the witches and the murder plan (Acts 1-2)
lessons.title: Macbeth: Shakespeare, Jacobean England and the exam
objectives: Explain key Jacobean contexts that shape Macbeth
Understand how Section A of Paper 1 is assessed

keywords.def: a play in which a great person falls because of a flaw and their choices
the belief that a king is chosen by God and must not be challenged
the killing of a king
a tragic flaw that leads to a hero's downfall
from the reign of James I (1603-1625)

starter: Bismillah. State what AO1, AO2 and AO3 each reward.
Which stave of A Christmas Carol shows Scrooge's redemption? Name one quotation.
Define 'context' and give one example from Dickens's Victorian Britain.

teach.heading: From Dickens to Shakespeare
bullets: Paper 1 has two sections: Shakespeare and the 19th-century novel
Section B was A Christmas Carol
Section A is Macbeth
Closed book: quotations must be learnt
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and link to Year 10: pupils have studied Section B. Explain that this half term they study Macbeth for Section A. Reassure them that the skills (point, quotation, zoom in, context) are the same. Emphasise that they will learn short, flexible quotations.

teach.heading: King James I
bullets: James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603
He was fascinated by witchcraft: Daemonologie (1597)
He had survived plots and feared assassination
Macbeth was probably written around 1606
teach.note: Explain that Shakespeare's company became the King's Men under James. Ask: why would a playwright flatter the king? Banquo was thought to be an ancestor of the Stuart line, so Banquo is presented as noble. Do not overstate: historians debate details, so say 'probably'.

teach.heading: The Gunpowder Plot and treason
bullets: The Gunpowder Plot (1605) tried to blow up Parliament and the king
Regicide was seen as the worst crime
Play shows the chaos that follows killing a king
The Porter scene refers to treason and equivocation
teach.note: Link the play's horror of regicide to the 1605 plot. Explain 'equivocation' as saying something misleading while claiming not to lie; it was discussed at the trials after the Plot. Ask: how does the play warn the audience about the consequences of treason?

teach.heading: Divine right and the Great Chain of Being
bullets: Kings were seen as God's representatives
The Great Chain of Being: God, angels, kings, nobles, people, animals
Killing a king disturbs the natural order
Expect storms and strange events after Duncan's death
teach.note: Explain the Jacobean idea of order. When Macbeth kills Duncan, the natural world goes wrong (an owl kills a falcon; horses eat each other). Ask pupils to predict how Shakespeare will show disorder.

teach.heading: The exam: Section A
bullets: One question on an extract and the whole play
About 50 minutes
AO1: 12 marks, AO2: 12, AO3: 6, AO4: 4
AO4 rewards spelling, punctuation and vocabulary accuracy
teach.note: Explain the structure: 'Starting with this extract... write about how the writer presents X in this extract and in the play as a whole.' Note total for Section A is 34 marks. Link to Y10: they used AO1-3 for Section B; Section A has the additional AO4 marks for accurate SPaG. Preview the character of Macbeth as a tragic hero.

practice: Explain why James I's interest in witchcraft matters for Macbeth.
What was the Gunpowder Plot and why might it matter to the play?
State what AO4 rewards.
independent: Make a mind map of three Jacobean contexts and a prediction for how each appears in the play.
Write a paragraph explaining 'divine right of kings' in your own words.
Write two questions you want answered about Macbeth.
exit: Name one context link to Macbeth you will remember.
lessons.homework: Read Act 1 scenes 1-3 and summarise the main events in five bullet points.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a context fact sheet with key terms and pictures; read the play in simplified summary alongside the text. Stretch: research and write a paragraph on how Shakespeare might have flattered King James.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Macbeth - Context, the witches and the murder plan (Acts 1-2)
lessons.title: Act 1: the witches, the prophecy and Macbeth's ambition
objectives: Analyse how Shakespeare presents the witches and the prophecy
Explore Macbeth's initial reaction and what it reveals about his ambition

keywords.def: a prediction about the future
a statement that seems to contradict itself but contains truth
words spoken to the audience that other characters cannot hear
a rhythm of four stressed beats beginning on a stress, used for the witches' speech
a strong desire to achieve power or success

starter: Bismillah. Name two contexts that shape Macbeth.
Define 'tragic hero'.
What is 'regicide'?

teach.heading: Opening in chaos
bullets: 1.1: thunder, lightning and three witches
"Fair is foul, and foul is fair"
Paradox: good and evil are confused
Short rhyming lines sound like a spell
teach.note: Read 1.1 aloud in a chant. Ask: why start with the witches before any human character? Explain that the paradox 'fair is foul' warns that appearances will deceive; this is a key theme (appearance and reality). Note the different rhythm of the witches' speech.

teach.heading: Macbeth the soldier
bullets: 1.2: the captain praises "brave Macbeth"
He kills Macdonwald in battle
Duncan rewards him with the title Thane of Cawdor
He is loyal and heroic before he meets the witches
teach.note: Briefly narrate 1.2. The violent language ('unseamed him from the nave to the chaps') shows Macbeth's skill and also foreshadows later violence. Ask: is he admired? Establish the 'before' picture so pupils can trace the change.

teach.heading: Meeting the witches
bullets: "So foul and fair a day I have not seen"
Macbeth echoes the witches' language
They greet him: Glamis, Cawdor, king hereafter
Banquo: "Lesser than Macbeth, and greater"
teach.note: Point out that Macbeth's first words echo the witches', suggesting a connection. Ask: why is Macbeth 'rapt' and 'starts' while Banquo is sceptical? Banquo's questions show a different response to temptation. Mention Qur'an 27:65: only Allah knows the unseen. In Jacobean Christian thought, trusting prophecies from dark powers is dangerous; as a class discuss temptation and free will with respect.

teach.heading: Ambition and choice
bullets: Macbeth: "If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me"
Then he thinks of murder: "horrid image"
Aside: "Stars, hide your fires"; he hides "black and deep desires"
Dark imagery shows he knows it is wrong
teach.note: Track Macbeth's changing thoughts: first leaving it to chance, then imagining murder, then wanting to hide his desires. Zoom in on 'black and deep desires': what does the adjective suggest? Link to hamartia: ambition without moral limits.

teach.heading: Planning a paragraph
bullets: Point: Shakespeare presents ambition as dangerous
Quotation: "black and deep desires"
Zoom in: dark imagery, secrecy
Link: context of treason and divine order
teach.note: Model a paragraph and highlight each part. Emphasise that pupils must analyse words and techniques, not retell. Ask for improvements to the model. Link to the idea that the witches tempt but Macbeth chooses.

practice: Explain what the paradox 'Fair is foul, and foul is fair' suggests.
Why does Banquo react differently to the prophecy?
What does 'black and deep desires' suggest about Macbeth's thoughts?
independent: Write a paragraph analysing how Shakespeare presents the witches in Act 1.
Write a paragraph on Macbeth's first reaction to the prophecy, with two embedded quotations.
Label the techniques you used.
exit: Define 'paradox' and give the example from 1.1.
Is Macbeth wholly responsible for his choices? Give one reason.
lessons.homework: Learn three quotations from Act 1 and write them from memory.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a scene summary and highlighted key lines; use a paragraph frame. Stretch: compare Macbeth's and Banquo's responses to the prophecy in a paragraph with evaluative comment.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Macbeth - Context, the witches and the murder plan (Acts 1-2)
lessons.title: Act 1: Lady Macbeth, Duncan and the decision to kill
objectives: Analyse how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth in Act 1
Explain the arguments for and against the murder in Macbeth's soliloquy

keywords.def: a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts alone on stage
a command, such as 'Come'
the roles and expectations linked to men and women
controlling someone through persuasion or pressure

starter: Bismillah. What does 'Fair is foul' mean?
Name one quotation showing Macbeth's ambition.
Define 'soliloquy'.

teach.heading: Lady Macbeth reads the letter
bullets: 1.5: she learns of the prophecy
She fears his nature is "too full o' the milk of human kindness"
She believes Macbeth is too gentle
She decides to push him
teach.note: Read the letter and her reaction. 'Milk of human kindness' means natural compassion; she sees it as a weakness. Ask: how is she presented as more ruthless than her husband? Highlight that she is the one who plans.

teach.heading: Calling on dark forces
bullets: "unsex me here"
Imperatives: "Come, you spirits"
She wants to remove feminine qualities
Context: Jacobean women expected to be gentle
teach.note: Zoom in on 'unsex me here': she wants to be free from compassion. Discuss gender expectations in 1606. Ask whether she is powerful or whether she must reject womanhood to gain power. Note that the invocation of evil spirits would shock a Jacobean audience.

teach.heading: Appearance and reality
bullets: "Look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't"
Serpent recalls the Garden of Eden
She teaches Macbeth to deceive
False hospitality towards Duncan
teach.note: Link the serpent imagery to the biblical fall. Ask what her advice reveals about the theme of appearance and reality. Compare with the witches' paradox. Show how she controls the plan: 'Leave all the rest to me'.

teach.heading: Macbeth's doubts
bullets: 1.7 soliloquy: reasons not to kill
Duncan is king, kinsman and guest
Duncan's virtues "will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued"
No reason but "vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself"
teach.note: Read the soliloquy aloud. List Macbeth's moral reasons. Explain the horse-riding metaphor: ambition leaps too high and falls. This is a key quotation for a thesis on ambition's danger. Note that he states the reasons clearly, so he knows it is wrong.

teach.heading: Persuasion and masculinity
bullets: She questions his courage and manhood
"screw your courage to the sticking-place"
"I dare do all that may become a man"
Who is really in control?
teach.note: Show how she manipulates through challenging his masculinity. Macbeth's reply defines manhood as moral limits. Ask: does she persuade him or does he choose? Prepare pupils to say 'how far' she is powerful: a judgement for the exam.

practice: Explain what 'unsex me here' suggests about Lady Macbeth's attitude to gender.
What does 'Look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't' show about appearance and reality?
Why does Macbeth hesitate in 1.7?
independent: Write two paragraphs on how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth in Act 1, with embedded quotations and a context link.
Write a short paragraph on how far Macbeth is responsible for the murder.
Highlight the AO1, AO2 and AO3 in your writing.
exit: Write one embedded quotation about Lady Macbeth.
lessons.homework: Learn two quotations from Lady Macbeth and write a short analysis of each word you find most important.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a quotation bank with word-level notes; allow bullet-point planning. Stretch: evaluate whether Lady Macbeth is more guilty than Macbeth.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Macbeth - Context, the witches and the murder plan (Acts 1-2)
lessons.title: Act 2: the dagger, the murder and guilt
objectives: Analyse the dagger soliloquy and the murder scene
Explore how Shakespeare introduces guilt and disorder

keywords.def: seeing something that is not really there
hints about what will happen later
an idea or image that recurs throughout a text
nature reflecting human mood or events

starter: Bismillah. Name one reason Macbeth hesitates before murder.
Quote Lady Macbeth's advice about appearing innocent.
What is a motif?

teach.heading: The dagger soliloquy
bullets: "Is this a dagger which I see before me"
Hallucination: guilt or the supernatural?
Questions show his confusion
The dagger leads him to Duncan
teach.note: Read the soliloquy and act it out in pairs. Ask: is the dagger real, supernatural or a product of his conscience? Explain the effect of questions and the movement from doubt to resolve. Note the bell: the signal that begins the killing.

teach.heading: The murder offstage
bullets: Duncan is killed offstage
Audience hears only sounds: owl, cry, bell
"Had he not resembled / My father as he slept"
She too has limits
teach.note: Explain that the murder is not shown; the imagination makes it worse and the audience is not alienated by gore. Highlight Lady Macbeth's brief humanity ('resembled my father'). Pupils should see that she is not as hard as she claims.

teach.heading: Guilt appears at once
bullets: "Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep"
"Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?"
Hyperbole shows overwhelming guilt
Lady Macbeth: "A little water clears us of this deed"
teach.note: Analyse the sleep motif: the murder of Duncan asleep destroys Macbeth's peace. Zoom in on 'Neptune's ocean' and 'incarnadine': the blood would turn the sea red. Contrast Lady Macbeth's practical 'a little water', and note how this contrast returns in Act 5 when she cannot wash her hands. Link to the hadith about the sincerity of intention: actions are judged by intentions (Bukhari and Muslim): the play explores how intention and guilt are bound together.

teach.heading: Disorder in nature
bullets: Night of storm, unnatural noises
Ross: "dark night strangles the travelling lamp"
Porter scene: hell-gate and equivocation
Link to the Great Chain of Being
teach.note: Discuss how nature reacts to regicide. Mention the Porter's humour and how it offers relief but also links Macbeth's castle to hell. Ask pupils to find evidence of disorder. Link to context: divine right.

teach.heading: Write about the murder
bullets: Point: guilt begins immediately
Quote: "Sleep no more"
Zoom in: sleep motif, short sentence, repetition
Link: guilt as punishment for treason
teach.note: Model a P.Q.Z.L paragraph and ask pupils to annotate. Emphasise the word 'immediately': guilt arrives before the crime is complete. Encourage a conceptual thesis: Shakespeare presents guilt as an inevitable consequence of unnatural acts.

practice: Why is the dagger soliloquy effective as a way of showing Macbeth's state of mind?
What does 'Sleep no more' suggest?
How does Lady Macbeth's reaction to the blood differ from Macbeth's?
independent: Write a paragraph on the dagger soliloquy, embedding two short quotations.
Write a paragraph on how guilt is presented in 2.2.
Write a context link about disorder after regicide.
exit: Define 'motif' and name one motif in Act 2.
Embed a short quotation about the blood.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word analysis of 'Will all great Neptune's ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?'
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the soliloquy with glossed words and a paragraph frame. Stretch: compare Macbeth's and Lady Macbeth's responses to guilt, with a brief judgement.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Macbeth - Tyranny, guilt and downfall (Acts 3-5)
lessons.title: Acts 3 and 4: tyranny, Banquo and the apparitions
objectives: Trace Macbeth's development from king to tyrant
Analyse the apparitions and the murder of Macduff's family

keywords.def: a cruel ruler who uses power unjustly
a ghostly appearance
using misleading language that avoids a direct lie
when the audience knows more than the characters
unreasonable fear that others are plotting against you

starter: Bismillah. Quote a line that shows guilt in 2.2.
What does 'motif' mean?
Which context idea explains disorder after Duncan's death?

teach.heading: Macbeth fears Banquo
bullets: 3.1: "To be thus is nothing; / But to be safely thus"
Banquo knows the prophecy
Macbeth hires murderers
He now acts without his wife's help
teach.note: Explain that Macbeth is king but insecure. The prophecy said Banquo's sons will be kings. Ask: how has Macbeth changed from Act 1? He now plans murder himself and keeps secrets from Lady Macbeth: 'Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck'.

teach.heading: Mental torment
bullets: "O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife!"
Image of poison and pain
He cannot enjoy kingship
Murder leads to more murder
teach.note: Zoom in on 'scorpions': the image of poison and torment. Contrast with the confident Macbeth of Act 1. Ask whether he is a victim or a villain.

teach.heading: Banquo's ghost
bullets: 3.4: the banquet
Only Macbeth sees the ghost
Lady Macbeth covers: "Sit, worthy friends"
"I am in blood / Stepped in so far" (3.4)
teach.note: Discuss whether the ghost is real or guilt. Note the contrast with Act 2: Lady Macbeth is now losing control. Analyse the river-of-blood metaphor: he cannot go back. This quotation is excellent for the idea that tyranny feeds itself.

teach.heading: The apparitions
bullets: 4.1: "Double, double toil and trouble"
Armed head: beware Macduff
Bloody child: "none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth"
Crowned child: safe until Birnam Wood moves
teach.note: Explain how the apparitions mislead through equivocation. Ask pupils how the prophecies could be true in an unexpected way. Mention that Macbeth trusts them too easily, increasing dramatic irony. Remind pupils of 27:65: knowledge of the unseen belongs to Allah, and so the play shows the folly of trusting dark powers.

teach.heading: Macduff's family
bullets: 4.2: Lady Macduff and her son are killed
Macbeth now kills innocents
Macduff: "All my pretty chickens and their dam"
Malcolm: "Let grief / Convert to anger"
teach.note: Discuss how this scene makes Macbeth a tyrant. The audience feels pity and anger. Point out the contrast between the family scene and Macbeth's violence. Link to the Jacobean view that a tyrant brings suffering to the whole country.

practice: How has Macbeth changed from Act 1 to Act 3?
Why is the ghost scene important?
Explain how the apparitions mislead Macbeth.
independent: Write a paragraph on how Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tyrant, with two quotations.
Write a paragraph on 'I am in blood / Stepped in so far'.
Explain how the apparitions create dramatic irony.
exit: Embed a quotation about the apparitions.
lessons.homework: Revise: write a timeline of Macbeth's murders and their motives.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a plot timeline and glossed quotations. Stretch: evaluate whether Macbeth is a victim of fate or responsible for his tyranny.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Macbeth - Tyranny, guilt and downfall (Acts 3-5)
lessons.title: Act 5: guilt, downfall and restoration of order
objectives: Analyse Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking and Macbeth's 'Tomorrow' soliloquy
Evaluate the ending and Malcolm's restoration of order

keywords.def: emotional release the audience feels at the end of a tragedy
the belief that life has no meaning
the return of proper rule after chaos
a comparison saying one thing is another

starter: Bismillah. Quote a line about Macbeth being stuck in violence.
What was Macbeth told by the apparitions?
Define 'dramatic irony'.

teach.heading: Lady Macbeth's sleepwalking
bullets: 5.1: "Out, damned spot! Out, I say!"
Prose, not verse: her mind breaks down
"All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand"
Compare 2.2: "A little water clears us of this deed"
teach.note: Read 5.1 slowly. Contrast the confident planner with the broken woman. Prose shows loss of control. Zoom in on 'perfumes of Arabia': even the richest fragrance cannot remove the stain of guilt. Link guilt to conscience and accountability.

teach.heading: Macbeth hears of her death
bullets: "She should have died hereafter"
"Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow / Creeps in this petty pace"
"Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player"
"a tale / Told by an idiot ... Signifying nothing"
teach.note: Analyse the repetition and rhythm of 'Tomorrow' that make time drag. Explain the metaphors: life as a shadow, an actor and a tale. He has lost all meaning. Ask: is this self-pity or truthful insight? Note the contrast with his heroic image in Act 1.

teach.heading: The illusion breaks
bullets: Birnam Wood moves: soldiers carry branches
Macduff: "was from his mother's womb / Untimely ripped"
Macbeth: "I'll not yield"
Fights to the end, still brave
teach.note: Explain how the prophecies are fulfilled in unexpected ways. Ask why the audience might feel some admiration for Macbeth's courage at the end. Link to tragedy: a hero with great qualities brought down by his flaw.

teach.heading: Restoration and Malcolm
bullets: Macbeth is killed offstage
Malcolm: "this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen"
Malcolm becomes king; Scotland is restored
Order returns: rightful succession
teach.note: Discuss how Malcolm's final speech restores order and reflects James I's ideal of a rightful king. Ask whether the ending is entirely positive: the language ('butcher', 'fiend-like') is harsh and arguably simplifies the story.

teach.heading: Evaluate the ending
bullets: Is Macbeth a villain or a tragic hero?
Evidence for both sides
Aim for a judgement in your essay
Link to context: punishment of regicide
teach.note: Prepare a balanced argument: villain because he chooses murder; tragic hero because of his conscience and bravery. Teach pupils to use phrases like 'arguably' and 'on one hand'. This builds the conceptual thesis they need for top marks.

practice: How does prose in 5.1 show Lady Macbeth's state of mind?
What does 'Life's but a walking shadow' suggest?
How does Malcolm describe Macbeth and why?
independent: Write a paragraph comparing Lady Macbeth in 2.2 and 5.1 with embedded quotations.
Write a paragraph analysing the 'Tomorrow' soliloquy.
Write a short evaluative paragraph: Is Macbeth a tragic hero?
exit: Give one quotation and say what it shows about Macbeth at the end.
lessons.homework: Learn three quotations from Act 5 and write an annotation for each.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the soliloquy with glossed words and structured notes. Stretch: write a conceptual thesis about the presentation of fate and choice across the play.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Macbeth - Themes and writing the Section A response
lessons.title: Themes and the whole-play view: ambition, kingship, the supernatural and appearance
objectives: Trace key themes across the whole play
Choose and link quotations from different acts

keywords.def: an idea that runs throughout a text
a repeated image or idea such as blood, sleep or darkness
your central argument in an essay
placing two contrasting things side by side

starter: Bismillah. Quote a line from Act 1, Act 3 and Act 5.
Define 'tragic hero'.
Give two contexts that explain the play's attitude to kings.

teach.heading: Ambition
bullets: Act 1: "black and deep desires"
Act 1: "vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself"
Act 3: "safely thus"
Act 5: "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow"
teach.note: Trace the arc: ambition leads to murder, insecurity, tyranny, emptiness. Show how pupils can link moments rather than listing them. Ask: does the play condemn ambition itself or ambition without morality?

teach.heading: Kingship
bullets: Duncan: good, trusting king
Macbeth: usurper and tyrant
Malcolm: rightful heir, order restored
Edward the Confessor in England: a holy, healing king
teach.note: Explain that the English king in 4.3 is a model of good kingship, linking to James I. Compare the three Scottish kings. Pupils write a comparison sentence. Mention 'borrowed robes' (1.3) and 'a giant's robe / Upon a dwarfish thief' (5.2): clothing imagery shows Macbeth unfit to be king.

teach.heading: The supernatural
bullets: The witches tempt but do not force
Ghosts and apparitions: guilt or reality?
Jacobean fear of witchcraft
Free will and responsibility
teach.note: Revisit the witches. Ask: what do they do and what do they not do? They never tell Macbeth to murder. Discuss free will with respect; in Islam we believe that each person is accountable for their choices, and that knowledge of the unseen belongs to Allah alone.

teach.heading: Appearance and reality
bullets: "Fair is foul, and foul is fair"
"False face must hide what the false heart doth know"
Lady Macbeth: innocent flower, serpent
Duncan: "There's no art / To find the mind's construction in the face"
teach.note: Link quotations across acts. Duncan's line about trusting Cawdor (1.4) is ironic because he then trusts Macbeth. Ask pupils how this theme shapes plot and structure.

teach.heading: Build a whole-play argument
bullets: Choose a theme and a thesis
Select one quotation per act
Add one context link
Write a conceptual first sentence
teach.note: Model a thesis: 'Shakespeare presents ambition as a force that destroys both the individual and the kingdom.' Pupils add one quotation per act. Emphasise short quotations that can be reused across questions.

practice: Which quotation links best to the theme of kingship?
Give one example of the 'appearance and reality' theme from Act 1 and one from Act 5.
What is a thesis?
independent: Create a theme grid: ambition, kingship, supernatural, appearance and reality; one quotation per act for each.
Write a thesis for the theme of ambition.
Write a paragraph linking two moments from different acts.
exit: State one thesis about Macbeth in one sentence.
Name one motif and one example.
lessons.homework: Write a plan for 'How does Shakespeare present ambition in Macbeth?'
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a partly completed theme grid. Stretch: write an introduction with a sophisticated thesis and a brief reference to context.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Macbeth - Themes and writing the Section A response
lessons.title: Writing a Section A response: extract and whole play
objectives: Plan and write a full Section A response
Move smoothly from the extract to the whole play

keywords.def: a short passage printed on the exam paper
a quotation woven into your own sentence
a reasoned conclusion supported by evidence
accurate spelling, punctuation and vocabulary

starter: Bismillah. State what AO4 rewards.
Give a one-sentence thesis about ambition in Macbeth.
Name three short quotations you could use for Lady Macbeth.

teach.heading: Unpick the question
bullets: Starting with this speech, explain how far Lady Macbeth is presented as powerful
Part 1: the extract (1.5: "unsex me here")
Part 2: the play as a whole
Key words: how far, presents, powerful
teach.note: Display the full sample question: 'Starting with this speech, explain how far you think Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a powerful woman. Write about: how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth in this speech; how Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth in the play as a whole.' Underline 'how far': it invites a judgement and often both sides. The extract is Lady Macbeth's speech from 1.5; use your class edition. Remind pupils the paper is closed book, so they must rely on learnt quotations plus the printed extract.

teach.heading: Plan in five minutes
bullets: Thesis: powerful but ultimately destroyed
Extract points: commands and dark imperatives
Whole-play points: persuades Macbeth, then collapses
Context link for each point
teach.note: Model a plan with three or four paragraphs. Show how to move chronologically through the play after the extract. Include a short conclusion with a judgement.

teach.heading: Model paragraph
bullets: Point answering 'how far'
Embedded quotation: "unsex me here"
Zoom in: imperative, verb choice, effect
Link to context or to the whole play
teach.note: Read a model: 'Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as powerful in her determination to reject her gender: her demand to be "unsex[ed]" suggests she believes compassion is a weakness. The imperative "Come" shows her commanding spirits, which would shock a Jacobean audience.' Pupils annotate the model. Stress analysing words.

teach.heading: Link to the whole play
bullets: Use phrases: later in the play...
Show development, not just a list
Compare early and late moments
Refer to 2.2 and 5.1
teach.note: Link: her control in 1.7 contrasts with the sleepwalking of 5.1, which shows power is temporary. Teach pupils to avoid retelling. Short quotations are enough.

teach.heading: Check against the mark scheme
bullets: AO1: personal response with quotations
AO2: language, form and structure
AO3: context woven into analysis
AO4: accurate SPaG; about 50 minutes
teach.note: Share a simplified mark scheme. Pupils check plans against the AOs, then write. Remind them to leave 3-5 minutes to proofread for AO4: capital letters, apostrophes, spelling of character and play names. End with dua for exam success if appropriate.

practice: Write a one-sentence thesis in answer to the sample question.
Write the first sentence of a paragraph that moves from the extract to the play.
Write an embedded quotation about Lady Macbeth.
independent: Write a full response (about 35 minutes) to the Lady Macbeth question.
Highlight your thesis, three quotations and two context links.
Write one target based on the AO checklist.
exit: State the two parts of the Section A question.
Name one way you will gain AO4 marks.
lessons.homework: Redraft one paragraph, improving analysis of a single word and adding a link to the whole play.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: allow a paragraph frame and quotation bank; split the response across two sittings. Stretch: add an evaluative sentence on how far Lady Macbeth remains powerful by Act 5.
